title: Qualitative Approach
text:
Before we try to analyze a inital value problem like: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y), \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] using a qualitative or numerical approach, it is important to know the answer to two questions:

Does a solution exist?
Are solutions unique?

Answering yes to the first question means that there is a function \(y(t)\) defined on some open interval \(I\subset \mathbb R\) containing \(t_0\) that satisfies both the initial condition and the differential equation for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).
The following example illustrates what can go wrong.



Explain why the initial value problem (note how it is written a different way!): \[y\cdot\frac{dy}{dt}-1 = 0, \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] has no solution when \(y_0=0\).
Explain why the initial value problem: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=\text{sign}(t), \quad y(t_0)=y_0\] has no solution when \(t_0=0\).

Warning: If a solution exists, it does not necessarily mean it will be defined for all time!



Solve the initial value problem \[\frac{dy}{dt} = 1+y^2, \quad y(0)=0\]. Determine the interval of existence for \(y(t)\), i.e. the largest possible open interval \(I\) containing \(t=0\) on which the solution \(y(t)\) is defined.
The second question we have to address is whether or not a solution to an initial value problem is unique.
This is particularly important for mathematical modeling. If we are using a differential equation to try and predict how some real world system will evolve, we want to know that that our model predicts a unique outcome!
The following example illustrates how uniqueness can fail.



Find at least two functions \(y(t)\) satisfying the initial value problem: \[\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{2/3}, \quad y(1)=0\].

Revisiting Slope Fields

Problem 4: Temperature Change
Suppose you lost power inside your home and the temperature inside the building is changing as heat is exchanged through the exterior of the building.
Let \(B\) be the temperature inside your home and \(E\) be the temperature outside your home. Assume that:

The external temperature \(E\) is constant.
The rate of change of the temperature inside your home is proportional to the difference between the external and internal temperatures.

Based on these assumptions:

Write a differential equation modeling the rate of change of the temperature inside of your home.
Sketch the slope field for this differential equation.
Explain the different scenarios for how \(B(t)\) is expected to change as \(t\to\infty\).
Explain how you are implicitly using the Existence and Uniqueness theorems in your conclusions for part (c).
Now suppose \(E\) is not constant but fluctuates sinusoidally over time, e.g. \[E(t)=A\sin(k(t-T))+E_T\] what effect does this have on the long-term behavior of \(B(t)\)? Again, use a slope field to help you make your guess. Here is a link to a Desmos graph you can modify to help you make your conclusions.

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text: To introduce the course, we are going to start with an example that illustrates the process for modeling relationships between variables with differential equations. Before diving into our example, two questions need to be addressed:

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
What is a Differential Equation?
A differential equation establishes a relationship between one or more variables and their rates of change. You are already familiar with one type of differential equation from calculus:






NoteExample: Antiderivatives



Given a continuous function \(f(t)\), find all functions \(y(t)\) such that \[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t)\] for all \(t\) in some interval.


In your calc classes, you likely saw three techniques for finding \(y(t)\):

Qualitative Approach: Curve Sketching.

Since \(f(t)\) shows us the slope of \(y(t)\), we can deduce enough information from \(f(t)\) to sketch out a graph illustrating the behavior of \(y(t)\) like:

where it is increasing/decreasing
locations of local and possibly global extrema
concavity and the location of points of inflection


Algebraic Approach: Integration Techniques.

The rules of differentiation are concrete. If we are proficient with them, we can play an educated guess and check game to find \(y(t)\).
Standard integration techniques use rules for differentiation in clever ways to manipulate the problem into something more easily recognizable, e.g. \(u\)-substitution is based on the chain rule and integration by parts is based on the product rule.

Numerical Approach: FTC + Riemann Sums.

The fundamental theorem of calculus tells us that a solution to this problem always exists and gives us a procedure for constructing it: \[y(t)=C+\int_a^t f(x)dx \]
If we can’t find a “nice”1 formula for \(y(t)\) (i.e. some finite combination of elementary functions), we can always write out the integral formula and evaluate it using numerical techniques, like Riemann Sums.

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
What will we study?
What is new in this class is that the kinds of differential equations we want to solve will depend explicitly on the dependent variable. Our focus will be on ordinary differential equations (ODEs); ODEs can involve multiple dependent variables, however, they depend only on a single independent variable, usually thought of as time.
Equations where there are multiple independent variables (e.g. time and space) will involve partial derivatives, which is the focus of MATH-451 Partial Differential Equations (or PDEs).
We will start out with first-order equations, those that involve only the first derivative, and can be written in the form:






NoteFirst-Order Equations



Find \(y:I\subseteq\mathbb R\to \mathbb R\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C\)) such that
\[\frac{dy}{dt}=f(t,y)\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).


Later on, we will discuss first-order systems, which will involve several dependent variables, each with an equation for its derivative. We can write these systems succinctly in vector form in terms of a vector-valued function \(\mathbf{v}(t)\):






NoteFirst-Order Systems



Find \(\mathbf{v}: I\subseteq\mathbb R\to \mathbb R^n\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C^n\)) such that \[\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt}=f(t,\mathbf{v})\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).


We will also discuss second-order equations (and maybe a few second-order systems), which add second derivatives into the mix:






NoteSecond-Order Equations



Find \(y:I\subseteq\mathbb R \to \mathbb R\) (or maybe \(\mathbb C\)) such that \[\frac{d^2y}{dt^2}=f\left(t,y,\frac{dy}{dt}\right)\] for all \(t\) in the interval \(I\).

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
What is a Mathematical Model?
Differential equations are interesting enough on their own. However, the reason they were discovered and continue to be an area of active research is that they provide the right mathematical framework for modeling so many different real-world relationships. The key idea is that we can start with this local property—some formula governing the rate at which the variables in our system are changing—and use it to build a global model for how the system will evolve. This allows us to make predictions, weigh and compare decisions, simulate experiments, and try to discover properties that may otherwise be difficult or costly to observe.
This semester, we will frequently use the goal of modeling to help motivate the mathematical concepts involved with analyzing and solving differential equations. Our first example will walk us through the steps involved:

Create the Model.
Analyze the Model.
Interpret the Model.

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
Step 1: Creating the Model

Ask & Observe

Creating a model starts with a question. What is it that you want to understand better? Identify the variables of interest. Make observations and/or collect data to begin to think about what governs the rates at which these quantities change.

Make Assumptions

It will usually be impossible to create a perfect mathematical representation of the relationship we are interested in exploring. Even if we could, it will likely be too complex with too many variables to be able to extract something useful when we analyze it.
So, before writing down our equation or system of equations, we will need to make some simplifying assumptions. The simpler the equation, the easier it is to analyze, but we likely will also take away less from the analysis that we can use to address our motivating questions.
In most cases, the best approach is to start with an oversimplified model, and then slowly make it more complex and realistic until you reach your mathematical breaking point.

State Clearly

State your motivating questions and the assumptions you are making. Write out the resulting differential equation, clearly defining all variables and parameters that are being used.

title: Modeling with Differential Equations
text:
Example: Sprint Speed
Our first example is to create a model for how a sprinter’s speed increases throughout a 100m race. Reasons why we may be interested in this:

To understand the human physiology of track athletes better
Insight on what training improvements to target to improve sprinter performance


Assumptions
In this scenario, our assumptions are:

Each sprinter’s acceleration \(a\) at any moment in time is determined by their mass \(m\) and the net horizontal force acting on them \(F\) by Newton’s second law of motion.
The net horizontal force \(F\) is the difference between a sprinter’s intrinsic propulsive force \(F_P\) and a resistive force \(F_R\).
The intrinsic propulsive force \(F_P\) is constant. It is determined by their mass and the raw acceleration \(P\) they could theoretically achieve under maximum effort and in the absence of resistive forces.
The resistive force \(F_R\) opposes the sprinter’s motion. We would expect that the resistive force would increase with the runner’s speed \(v\) and mass. Let’s assume the resistive force is proportional to both of these quantities; let \(k\) represent this proportionality constant.



Discussion Problem 1: Create the model

With these assumptions, write down an equation modeling the relationship between a sprinter’s acceleration and their speed during a race.
Identify and define any independent variables, dependent variables, and parameters in the model. Are we making any assumptions about the values of the parameters or variables in our model?
If mass is measured in kilograms (kg), distance in meters (m), and time in seconds (s), what units would make sense for the parameters/variables in the model?







TipAnswer:






Based on the listed assumptions, \[m\frac{dv}{dt}=mP-mkv\]
The independent variable is time \(t\) and the dependent variable is speed \(v\); the parameters all depend on the runner—mass \(m\), max effort acceleration \(P\), and the resistive force constant \(k\). The way we have set up this model, we are assuming all parameters are positive. Given the context
\(P\) is acceleration so it should be \(m/s^2\); \(k\) will be \(s^{-1}\).

title: First Order Equations
text:
Our first unit covers chapter 1 of our textbook, along with some topics from sections 7.1-3 and Appendices A and B.
Key Ideas:

Basic terminology associated with differential equations
Using differential equations to model relationships between variables
Three main approaches to analyzing differential equations: qualitative, numerical, and analytical

Qualitative approach for first-order equations:

Slope fields and Phase lines
Equilibria, stability, and bifurcation diagrams.

Numerical approach for first-order equations:

Euler’s method
Error & improvements on Euler’s method (Improved Euler’s method, Runge-Kutta)

Analytical approach for first-order equations:

Existence and uniqueness criteria
Separation of variables
Integrating factors
Change of variables, power series, other techniques as time allows

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text: Once we have converted our question into a clearly stated, well-defined math problem, we can begin to analyze it.

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Step 2: Analyze the Model
Just like in calculus, we use a three-pronged approach to analyze differential equations:

Qualitative Approach. What does the equation governing the slope of the model tell us about the properties of any solution? Can we sketch a graph of the solution? Can we determine the long-run behavior of a solution? How do the properties of a solution depend on the parameters in the model?
Numerical Approach. Is there a numerical method we can use to estimate the values of a solution? Can we determine error bounds for this method? How does the error or convergence of the method depend on initial values or parameters?

Analytical Approach. Do we know a solution exists? Given some initial state, is the solution unique? Is it possible to actually extract a formula for the model?

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Example: Sprint Speed Continued
Recall that our model for a sprinter’s speed throughout a 100m race is given by: \[m\frac{dv}{dt}=mP-kmv\] where \(m\) is the sprinter’s mass (in kg), \(P\) represents the max effort acceleration a sprinter can achieve (in m/s\(^2\)), and \(k\) is the proportionality constant for the resistive force (in s\(^{-1}\)).

Discussion Problem 1: Qualitative Analysis.
We will start by analyzing it qualitatively:

Describe how the sprinter’s speed is expected to change throughout the race according to the model. Will it increase? decrease?
Describe how the sprinter’s acceleration is expected to change throughout the race.
Sketch a graph of \(v(t)\). What do you expect to happen to \(v(t)\) in the long run, i.e. what is \[\lim_{t\to\infty}v(t)?\] What is the practical significance of this?







TipAnswer:





First, it helps to simplify the differential equation by dividing through by mass: \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\]

Note that \(\frac{dv}{dt}=0\) when \(v=\frac{P}{k}\). So, that means if the sprinter is ever going at this speed, they will stay at this speed for all time. A constant solution to a differential equation, like this one, is called a equilibrium solution.
If \(v>\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}<0\), and so at this speed, their speed will decrease.
If \(v<\frac{P}{k}\), then \(\frac{dv}{dt}>0\), and so at this speed, their speed will increase.
In context, their speed at the beginning of the race will be 0 and so this is telling us that their speed should increase throughout the race according to the model.
If \(v\) is increasing throughout the race, then their acceleration \[\frac{dv}{dt}=P-kv\] will decrease.
Here is a “sketch” of a solution using a slope or direction field. What this tells us is that as the race goes on, the runner’s speed will approach a threshold of \(P/k\).






Discussion Problem 2: Numerical Analysis.
Next, can we use our equation to make numerical estimates for how the value of \(v(t)\) will change throughout the race. Let’s assume that \(P=10\) \(m\cdot s^{-2}\) and \(k=0.85\) s\(^{-1}\) for a particular sprinter during a race. Assume that their speed, \(v\), is \(0\) \(m\cdot s^{-1}\) initially at \(t=0\) and that for \(t\geq 0\), their speed changes according to our model.
Use the information provided to determine/estimate the following values of \(v(t)\) and \(v'(t)\):

Discussion Problem 3: Analytical Analysis.
This particular model is an example of a separable equation. These types of equations can be solved using a technique called separation of variables.

After we discuss the idea, try and use this technique to solve the equation.
Once you have your general solution, try and solve the initial value problem, where we are looking for a solution to the equation such that \(v(0)=0\).

title: Analyze & Interpret the Model
text:
Step 3: Interpret the Model
The results of your mathematical analysis ultimately have to be reframed in the context of your model. What did you learn? How does it relate to your motivating questions? Do your assumptions place any limitations on what you can reasonably take away from your analysis?
If possible, compare how well your model fits real data. What can you learn from any discrepancies and how can you use this information to make your model better?
